block.text:
Now let's look at the functionality of opening the file and using it's contents using new functions:

import java.nio.file.*;
import java.io.IOException;

class FileExample {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        String contents = Files.readString(Paths.get("quotes.txt"));
        System.out.println(contents);

        String[] words = contents.split(" ");
        for (String word: words) {
            System.out.println(word);
        }
    }
}

 quotes.txt has the following contents:

All is well!
You got this!
This too shall pass!

If we then run this code in the Lecture 18 11pm workspace on EdStem we see that it has, in fact, read in the entire file and not just 1 line. Here is the output:

[user@sahara ~]$ java FileExample
All is well!
You got this!
This too shall pass!

All
is
well!
You
got
this!
This
too
shall
pass!

If you're wondering why the first thing it does is print an entire copy of quotes, it is because the first thing we wrote in our code after setting contents to readString of our file was to println(contents).

Also recall the description of readString was

Reads all content from a file into a string

and it has done exactly that. It reads the whole file, not stopping until End Of File (EOF) is reached. Then to print each word out on it's own line in the output we split on each space character and print.
